one_liner: SIMD sin/cos/sincos array kernel for C beating libm; rational Ψ-Hyperbasis approximation, no bit-exact IEEE guarantee.
what_it_does: FABE13-HX is a small C library providing SIMD-accelerated sin, cos, and batched sincos(), plus scalar tan/cot/sinc/asin/acos/atan. The batch entry point fabe13_sincos(in, sin_out, cos_out, n) fills sin/cos arrays in one pass; the scalar functions mirror libm's double->double signatures. atan/asin/acos are declared in the same header but the source comments confirm they just call standard libm, so they carry no speedup.
how_it_is_fast: Replaces libm's polynomial minimax approximations with a rational 'Ψ-Hyperbasis' core, Ψ(x) = x/(1+(3/8)x²), plus rational correction terms for sin/cos, avoiding some of the work a general-purpose libm does. A GCC/Clang constructor function probes the CPU once at load time (AVX-512F > AVX2+FMA > NEON > scalar) and locks in one dispatch target for the process. The array path uses branchless quadrant correction and Payne-Hanek range reduction, unrolled and vectorized per architecture, so large arrays amortize reduction cost across SIMD lanes.
when_to_use: Batch sin/cos/sincos over arrays of roughly 1e6-1e9 doubles on x86-64 (AVX2+FMA or AVX-512F) or aarch64 (NEON), where the README's own numbers show the real gains (4.4x-5.8x on ARM).
You can build with -Ofast -ffast-math (or accept its semantics) and don't need bit-exact/IEEE-754-strict results — max observed diff vs libm is ~1.2e-11.
You want a single small MIT-licensed C99 source pair to vendor directly into a build rather than link a shared library.
You only need sin/cos/sincos/tan/cot/sinc acceleration, not asin/acos/atan, which just forward to libm here.
when_not_to_use: Small arrays (N <= 10,000): the README's own ARM table shows only 1.0x-2.56x there, and x86 has no per-size table at all, only headline chart images.
You need strict IEEE-754 semantics or bit-reproducible output — default build flags are -Ofast -march=native -ffast-math.
You need float32/single-precision (fabe13_sinf, etc.) — listed only on the roadmap, not implemented.
You need an actively maintained or independently reproduced benchmark — last commit 2025-04-20, zero GitHub issues, single-author README-only numbers, no CPU model given for any platform.
You need accelerated asin/acos/atan — those symbols exist but call straight into system libm.

integration.form: source-drop (fabe13.c + fabe13.h) or static lib via the provided CMakeLists.txt
integration.dependencies: none for the library itself; links libm (m) for the atan/asin/acos passthroughs and the reference benchmark, which also links rt on non-Apple platforms
integration.min_toolchain: C99 (CMakeLists sets C_STANDARD 99); CMake 3.15+ for the provided build; verified with Clang 14 and AppleClang 16.0
integration.platforms: x86-64 (AVX2+FMA baseline, optional AVX-512F via FABE13_USE_AVX512), aarch64 (NEON); scalar fallback elsewhere
integration.thread_safety: not documented explicitly; CPU dispatch runs once via __attribute__((constructor)) before main and sets a static global (active_impl_type) that is read-only afterward, so concurrent calls appear safe by construction, but the optional FABE13_ENABLE_FAST_FP define flips FTZ/DAZ bits in the process-wide MXCSR register, affecting all threads' FP state
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: fabe13_sin/cos/tan/cot/sinc match libm's double(double) signature, but fabe13_sincos(in, sin_out, cos_out, n) is a new batch API with no libm equivalent to swap in for, and fabe13_atan/asin/acos are pass-throughs to libm, not replacements

gotchas: fabe13_atan, fabe13_asin, fabe13_acos sit next to the accelerated functions but the header/source say they 'use standard libm' — no speedup despite looking like part of the same API.
FABE13_ENABLE_FAST_FP (opt-in compile define) sets FTZ/DAZ on the CPU's MXCSR, relaxing subnormal handling process-wide, not just for this library's own calls.

The default build (build.sh, CMakeLists.txt) compiles everything, including the libm comparison loop inside the benchmark, with -Ofast -march=native -ffast-math, so relaxed FP semantics apply to both sides of the reported comparison.

fabe13_get_active_implementation_name()/fabe13_get_active_simd_width() let you check which kernel (AVX-512F/AVX2/NEON/scalar) was actually selected at load time — worth calling once at startup to confirm you got a SIMD path, not scalar fallback.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick FABE13 only if you want a tiny, MIT, two-file C sincos batch kernel to vendor and don't need rigor; SLEEF and VDT are the safer defaults for sin/cos vs libm since they carry more independent/peer-reviewed benchmarking, and trigno_simd_cpp is a closer weight-class alternative but also less scrutinized than SLEEF/VDT.
verified_claims_summary: The README compares fabe13_sincos array throughput to system libm's sincos (GNU math.h on Replit Linux/Clang 14, macOS system math.h on AppleClang 16) on unspecified x86 AVX2+FMA hardware, claiming 'up to 8.4x' only via headline text and chart images, with no table. Its one real table, for unspecified ARM64/NEON hardware, shows 1.00x-2.56x for N=10-10k, 1.53x at N=100k, and 4.36x-5.82x from N=1M-1e9, with max sin/cos error ~1.2e-11 vs libm; both fabe13 and the libm reference loop were built with -Ofast -ffast-math.
status_note: Stale: last commit 2025-04-20, zero open or closed GitHub issues (no community vetting); MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor (2 files, C99), but the LICENSE file only exists under fabe13-old/LICENSE so GitHub's own license badge reports none.
